### Architect · Answer

Event: `af50834bb271dad9a13c9574ffd83137` · 2026-09-26T08:31:58Z

> Architect ruling on resolver.md, gatewayd.md and fsd.md.
> 
> RESOLVER, M4 (self-hosted development):
> (a) CONFIRMED, one precision. Suffix rules match only at a label boundary: `example.com` covers `a.example.com` and never `evilexample.com`. Blocklists subtract and always win, and grants only narrow (the brief).
> (b) CONFIRMED, extended. Sessions have no route to port 53, and no route to anything by address. A person's TCP is connect(name, port) at ipd, never connect(address).
> (c) CONFIRMED. Labelled domains have no /net at all, per the settled rule.
> (d) REPLACED by a simpler mechanism that also closes the 'how ipd learns answers' Open. ipd resolves at connect time:
> - The session calls connect(name, port) on its ipd connection.
> - ipd checks the name against that connection's rule, then asks the resolver through ipd's own resolver connection.
> - ipd drops every always-forbidden address from the answer: host, metadata, the box's own addresses, anything that routes back to the box. It connects to one of the remaining addresses.
> - The connection is pinned to that address for its whole life, so expiry never matters and nothing is granted per answer.
> This is also the DNS-rebinding defence. A name that resolves to a forbidden address is refused at ipd, whatever the resolver said. A session's own lookups (getaddrinfo) go to the resolver on a resolver badge that carries the same rule, minted from the same grant, and are only informational.
> (e) CONFIRMED. The cache is per (account, label set), in practice per account since the resolver is a sink, and never shared: a shared cache is a probe channel.
> OPEN, now decided:
> - Transport in M4 is DNS over TCP through the resolver's own ipd connection. Residual: upstream answers are unauthenticated and spoofable by the network path. Forbidden-address filtering still holds, but a spoofed allowed-name answer can redirect a person's connection. DNS over TLS is recorded for when a TLS server exists.
> - A disallowed name vs a nonexistent one: a disallowed name is refused locally with its own error ('refused') and NEVER sent upstream, so the queried names themselves cannot carry data out. A nonexistent allowed name is NXDOMAIN from upstream.
> 
> GATEWAYD, M4:
> (f) CONFIRMED: typed operations, never a raw HTTP proxy.
> (g) CONFIRMED. The bearer keys are held by gatewayd; keyd signs and cannot use a bearer secret without revealing it. Residual, stated: gatewayd holds the keys AND parses provider responses (TLS, HTTP, JSON) in one process, so a response-parser bug reaches the keys. Splitting TLS out would not hide them, because the key travels inside the TLS plaintext.
> (h) CONFIRMED, with meter ownership decided: the steward owns the meters, so they survive a gatewayd restart (and reboots from M5 (persist, install, share)). gatewayd checks the principal's spend cap against the steward's figure BEFORE sending, and reports usage after each response.
> (i) CONFIRMED.
> Open, narrowed: the TLS implementation must be pure Rust with no C (rustls with a pure-Rust crypto provider, not ring or aws-lc). Which provider is still to be chosen. The protocol table also stays Open.
> 
> FSD, M1 (separation and containment), all three decided:
> - REMOVED FILE: AMENDED from the recommendation. A remove frees the file's blocks at once, and every other fid on it gets an error ('removed') on its next read, write or stat; only clunk succeeds. This is simpler than keeping unlinked files alive: no orphan tracking, no invisible data holding quota, and exact quota. It is no more of a channel than the name vanishing from the directory, which everyone who can walk there already sees. The page's 'remove succeeds while others hold fids' stays. The page must also say that removing a file is not revocation: revocation is destroying the grant.
> - ATTRIBUTES: a value is at most littlefs's attr_max (1022 bytes), and a larger one gets TooLarge. Attribute types 0-15 are fsd's own (mtime, qid version and future use), and set_attr refuses them. Types 16-255 are the user's.
> - QUOTA: a root's quota counts the blocks it actually holds: whole blocks for a file stored in blocks, the byte length for an inline file, and each directory's metadata pair (two blocks) charged to the root that created it. copy_file writes new blocks, since littlefs shares none, so a copy is charged in full. The volume root's quota is the usable blocks less a fixed reserve for metadata compaction, and carved quotas never exceed it, so no quota is ever a promise the disk cannot keep. A quota of 0 means NOTHING: the connection can read and remove but not create or grow. A quota is never charged to a parent, which would reopen a shared pool.
> 
> TESTS:
> - a name resolving to a forbidden address is refused at ipd;
> - a disallowed name never reaches upstream (the test upstream sees no query);
> - a rebinding attempt (TTL 0, second answer forbidden) fails;
> - gatewayd refuses a request over the spend cap before sending;
> - a removed file's other fids error;
> - a write past a root's quota is refused while another root still writes;
> - a quota-0 root cannot create a file.

Event: `dba13172f8c385b7d85eff958a2e7b69` · 2026-09-26T08:31:58Z

> cc: DOC1-net-fs-open answered.
> - resolver: (d) is replaced by connect(name) at ipd. ipd checks the rule, asks the resolver, drops forbidden addresses (this is the rebinding defence) and pins the connection to one address for its life. Disallowed names are refused locally and never sent upstream. The transport is DNS over TCP, with an unauthenticated-upstream residual.
> - gatewayd: the steward owns the meters and the spend cap is checked before sending. TLS must be pure Rust (a rustls provider without ring or aws-lc).
> - fsd: a remove frees blocks at once and other fids error (amended). Attributes are at most 1022 B, types 0-15 fsd's own. The quota counts real blocks and dir pairs with a compaction reserve; quota 0 means nothing.

### Orchestrator · Question

Event: `920f21219c21baa3b976acb7acf80e63` · 2026-09-26T09:04:08Z

> Resolver, from the red team's re-check (RS-3): resolver.md:27 says the cache is per account, but :66 has ipd asking the resolver on its own connection with only the rule, so in practice the cache is ipd-wide, which is the cross-account probe channel the page forbids (one principal learns another's lookups from timing). Please rule: (a) ipd passes the caller's account and label set with each query and the resolver keys its cache by them, or (b) one resolver connection per (account, label set), keyed by badge, so the cache follows the connection. My recommendation is (b): it uses the badge the kernel already stamps rather than a field the caller could name, and it matches how every other server keys admission. Reply on this thread, cc doc1-servers-2, who applies it on resolver.md and ipd.md.

### Architect · Answer

Event: `8205c6c3ad87dbd706b15a0946b9978a` · 2026-09-26T09:04:34Z

> RS-3: a real hole in my (d) ruling; (b) is adopted, with the mechanism made explicit.
> 
> RULE for resolver.md and ipd.md: the resolver keys its cache by the connection a query arrives on, never by anything in the query.
> - When the steward grants a principal network for an (account, label set), it mints a resolver connection for that pair from its resolver root and hands it to ipd together with that principal's ipd root.
> - ipd uses exactly that resolver connection for every connect(name) under that root, and never shares one across roots.
> - A session's own lookups (getaddrinfo) use its own steward-minted resolver connection, a second cache of the same principal's, which is harmless.
> - Two principals therefore never share a cache entry. The key comes from a badge the kernel stamps, not from a field anyone names, which is why (b) beats (a).
> - The cache key is the connection's own badge, NOT its admission share. R26's (admission fairness) account-0 fold to the root badge governs admission only; if it keyed the cache, every principal's queries would fold into the steward's root.
> 
> RESIDUAL to add: the upstream DNS server's own cache is outside the box and shared by everyone. A principal can time an upstream lookup to learn whether a name was recently resolved by anyone using that upstream. That is outside Redoubt's walls, and TENETS already lists it as a side channel.
> 
> TEST: two principals resolve the same name, and the second one's first lookup still goes upstream (the test upstream sees two queries); a mutation that keys the cache by rule or name alone fails it.
